prompt: After `Online` with a trailing space is typed into G4, the three channel totals add up to 51,379 and `=SUM(Sales[Revenue])` still says 51,494. Why?
hint: Which of the three `SUMIFS` asks for the word that is now in G4?

choices.text: SUM stopped counting sale S1003 as well
choices.why: SUM adds the Revenue column whatever the channel says, which is why it still shows 51,494.

choices.text: No SUMIFS asks for `Online ` with a space
choices.why: Right. The sale's 115 is still in the column and in SUM, and in no channel total.

choices.text: Excel turned the revenue of S1003 into text
choices.why: The revenue cell did not change; only the channel cell did.

choices.text: The trailing space made Excel count S1003 twice
choices.why: Nothing is counted twice: the channel totals came out lower, not higher.

prompt: With `Online ` (trailing space) in G4, what does `=SUMIFS(Sales[Revenue], Sales[Channel], "Online")` return?
hint: The Online total was 11,143, and S1003's revenue is 115.

prompt: Which of these values typed into G4 would the Online `SUMIFS` still count?
hint: `SUMIFS` compares the whole text, and one thing about letters it ignores.

choices.text: `Onlnie`
choices.why: Two letters swapped make a different word, and SUMIFS finds no match.

choices.text: `online`
choices.why: Right. SUMIFS does not care about capitals, so this one is still counted. It is the only one of the four.

choices.text: `Online ` with a trailing space
choices.why: The space is a character, so the word no longer matches; that is the lesson's example.

choices.text: `Web`, which means the same channel
choices.why: A person reads Web as Online; a formula only compares the text.

prompt: Match each value typed without a rule to where it does its damage.
hint: Ask which kind of formula reads that column.

pairs.right: A total by channel leaves the sale out
Every sum and average of bags is inflated
Totals by year and filters on dates go wrong
A lookup on the product answers #N/A

right_distractors: Excel refuses to save the workbook

prompt: Why does the lesson make `New sales` a table before putting any rule on it?
hint: Think about the row the next sale is typed in.

choices.text: A table column passes its rule to every new row
choices.why: Right. Type a sale under the table, the row joins it, and the rules come with it.

choices.text: Excel allows validation only on cells that are inside a table
choices.why: Any cell can hold a rule; the table is about rows that do not exist yet.

choices.text: A table makes the sheet read-only
choices.why: A table is as editable as any range.

choices.text: So that the new sales are copied into the Sales table by themselves
choices.why: Nothing in New sales reaches Sales; the lesson says so at the end.

prompt: The custom rule on the `Sale` column was written with A2 selected. When somebody types in A5, which cell does the rule's `LEN(A2)` read?
hint: A custom rule moves the way a formula moves when it is filled down.

choices.text: A2, always
choices.why: That would be true of $A$2. A2 is relative, so it moves with the row.

choices.text: A1, the header
choices.why: Nothing moves the reference upwards; it follows the row being typed.

choices.text: A5
choices.why: Right. The rule is read as if it had been filled down from A2 to A5.

choices.text: Every cell of column A at once
choices.why: LEN takes one cell. COUNTIF(A:A, …) is the part that looks at the whole column.

prompt: Why is the upper bound of the `Date` rule `=TODAY()` rather than today's date typed into the box?
hint: What happens to a typed date tomorrow?

choices.text: TODAY() moves every day, so nobody edits the rule
choices.why: Right, and a formula also avoids the question of how a typed date is read in each region.

choices.text: A date typed in that box makes Excel refuse every date entered
choices.why: A typed date works; it simply stops moving, and tomorrow's sales are refused.

choices.text: TODAY() is the only formula the box accepts
choices.why: The box takes any formula, which is why DATE(2025,1,1) is in the other one.

choices.text: It lets past dates through and stops only today's
choices.why: Between DATE(2025,1,1) and TODAY() includes today and every day since 2025 began.

prompt: `Bags` has the rule Whole number, between 1 and 50. Which of these typed values are refused? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two conditions: a whole number, and inside the bounds, which are included.

choices.why: Not a whole number.
Between includes its bounds, so 50 is accepted.
Below the lower bound of 1.

choices.text: `fourteen`
choices.why: Text is not a number at all.
A whole number inside the bounds: exactly what the rule wants.

prompt: `S1109` is typed in A2 of `NewSales` and accepted. Somebody then types `S1109` in A3. What does the Sale rule do?
hint: Count how many times column A holds the code at the moment A3 is checked.

choices.text: Accepts it, because S1109 is not in Sales
choices.why: That is one of three conditions. The third asks for the code once in this sheet, and it is now there twice.

choices.text: Refuses it: COUNTIF(A:A, A3) is 2
choices.why: Right. The cell being typed counts as the one, and A2 makes two.

choices.text: Accepts it and removes the code from A2
choices.why: Validation never changes another cell; it only judges the one being typed.

choices.text: Refuses it, because codes have to be in order
choices.why: No condition says anything about order.

prompt: A Custom validation rule lets a value in when its formula answers ___.
hint: One of the two logical values.

prompt: Why does the lesson create the name `ProductCodes` instead of typing `=Products[Code]` in the Source box?
hint: One of the two is refused by the box in most versions.

choices.text: A name is shorter to type
choices.why: It is, but the lesson's reason is that the box accepts it at all.

choices.text: The Source box refuses `=Products[Code]` and takes a name
choices.why: Right. The name keeps the table column's growth and gets past the box.

choices.text: A name freezes the list at six codes
choices.why: The opposite: the name points at the column, however long it grows.

choices.text: Names are recalculated faster than tables, so the list opens faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

prompt: Café Serra adds a seventh product as a new row of the `Products` table. A drop-down whose Source is `=Products!$A$2:$A$7` shows how many codes?
hint: Count the cells in the address.

choices.text: Seven, because the table grew
choices.why: The table grew, but the address names six fixed cells.

choices.text: None, because the address now points at the wrong rows
choices.why: The address still points at A2:A7, which still hold the first six codes.

choices.text: Six; the new product is missing from it
choices.why: Right. Only a reference to the column, through a name, grows with the table.

choices.text: Seven, as soon as the file is saved
choices.why: Saving does not change an address.

prompt: What does `=ROWS(CustomerCodes)` return, with the name pointing at `Customers[Customer]`?
hint: The customers run from C00.

prompt: In an Excel set to Portuguese, how are the items of a list typed straight into the Source box separated?
hint: The same character that separates a formula's arguments there.

choices.text: With commas, in every language
choices.why: That is the English separator; it follows the one the formulas use.

choices.text: With semicolons
choices.why: Right: `Wholesale;Online;Shop`.

choices.text: With spaces
choices.why: A space would be part of an item, which is exactly the typo validation is there to stop.

choices.text: One per line, with Enter
choices.why: Enter closes the dialog; the items go on one line.

prompt: Match each error alert style to what the person typing can do when the value breaks the rule.
hint: Only one style makes the value leave for good.

pairs.right: Retype it or cancel; the value cannot stay
Yes keeps it, No returns to edit it
OK keeps it, Cancel removes it

right_distractors: Excel corrects the value by itself

prompt: Somebody types a price in `NewSales` before choosing the product, so D2 is empty. What does the Price rule do?
hint: What does XLOOKUP answer when it looks up nothing, and how does a rule read an error?

choices.text: Accepts the price, because an empty product means no comparison
choices.why: There is a comparison, and its lookup fails.

choices.text: Excel picks the first product in the list for the lookup
choices.why: XLOOKUP looks up exactly what is in D2, which is nothing.

choices.text: Warns: the lookup answers #N/A, which counts as broken
choices.why: Right. Typing left to right, product first, avoids it.

choices.text: Refuses it with Stop, whatever the style says
choices.why: The style chosen is the one used; here it is Warning.

prompt: Which error alert style fits a product code that is not in the `Products` table?
hint: Is there ever a legitimate sale of a product that does not exist?

choices.text: Information, so the person knows
choices.why: OK keeps the value, and a sale of a nonexistent product enters the data.

choices.text: Warning, since some codes are new
choices.why: A new product enters the table first, and then the list offers it.

choices.text: Stop
choices.why: Right. The value is never legitimate, and Stop is the only style that enforces anything.

choices.text: No alert at all; the drop-down is enough
choices.why: The arrow offers values, and the alert is what refuses one typed by hand.

prompt: With the rule `=F2>=0.8*XLOOKUP(D2, Products!A:A, Products!F:F)`, what is the lowest price accepted without a warning for `CER1K`, whose list price is 118?
hint: 80% of the list price.

prompt: The Price rule's style is Warning. Somebody types `-5` and presses Yes. What is in the cell?
hint: One rule per cell, one style per rule.

choices.text: -5: Yes keeps it
choices.why: Right. That is the price of choosing Warning, and the lesson chose it for the commoner slip.

choices.text: Nothing, because negative numbers are always refused
choices.why: Only a rule refuses anything, and this one only warns.

choices.text: 5, because Excel drops the sign
choices.why: Validation never rewrites a value.

choices.text: The list price of the product
choices.why: Excel does not fill in a value for you.

prompt: A value is pasted with Ctrl+V into a `Bags` cell that has a rule. What happens?
hint: A plain paste brings more than the value.

choices.text: Excel checks it and shows the Stop message
choices.why: Only typing is checked.

choices.text: The value arrives unchecked, and the cell loses its rule
choices.why: Right. A plain paste replaces the cell's contents and its validation together.

choices.text: The paste is refused because the cell has a rule
choices.why: Excel pastes without asking the rule.

choices.text: The value arrives and a red circle appears round it
choices.why: Circles appear only when you ask for them with Circle Invalid Data.

prompt: Which of these reach a validated cell without the rule checking them? Choose all that apply.
hint: The rule acts at one moment only.

choices.text: A value pasted with Paste Special › Values
choices.why: The rule stays on the cell, and the pasted value is still not checked.

choices.text: A value typed and confirmed with Enter
choices.why: This is the one path the rule does check.

choices.text: A formula's answer that changes after a recalculation
choices.why: Formula results are never checked when they change.

choices.text: Values already in the cells when the rule was created
choices.why: A rule applies from then on; Circle Invalid Data finds the old ones.

prompt: With the rule Whole number between 1 and 15 on `Sales[Bags]`, how many cells does Circle Invalid Data circle?
hint: `=COUNTIF(Sales[Bags], ">15")` gives the same count.

prompt: Why does the lesson take the 1-to-15 rule off `Sales` after circling the four sales?
hint: What is `Sales` a record of?

choices.text: Those sales happened, and Sales records what happened
choices.why: Right. The rule was there to show Circle Invalid Data on old data, not to judge history.

choices.text: A rule on Sales would delete the four sales
choices.why: A rule never changes a value; it only judges typing.

choices.text: Circle Invalid Data works once per rule
choices.why: It works as often as you ask.

choices.text: Pivot tables refuse to read a column that has a validation rule on it
choices.why: A rule does not stop a pivot reading the column; the reason is about what Sales means.

prompt: Put the steps of a drop-down that grows with the `Customers` table in order.
hint: The rule needs something to point at before it can point at it.
items: Select the Customer cell of NewSales
Open Data › Data Validation and choose List
trap: Choosing List before the name exists leaves the Source box with nothing that grows.

prompt: A colleague puts a Whole number rule on a column of 500 imported rows and reports that the column is now validated. What is true?
hint: When does a rule look at a value?

choices.text: Every row was checked when the rule was created
choices.why: A rule checks typing from then on and looks at nothing already there.

choices.text: Rows breaking the rule were cleared
choices.why: Validation never changes or clears a value.

choices.text: Imported data cannot hold rules
choices.why: Any cell can hold a rule; the issue is that the rule has not looked at these values.

choices.text: None of the 500 rows was checked
choices.why: Right. The rule only guards what is typed next, and the circles show the old values that fail it.

prompt: Every morning somebody pastes the day's orders from an e-mail into `NewSales`. What makes the rules mean something for those rows?
hint: Ask which paste keeps the rules, and what checks a pasted value.

choices.text: Change every rule's style to Stop
choices.why: A paste never meets the alert, whatever its style.

choices.text: Untick Ignore blank on every rule
choices.why: That concerns empty cells; pasted values are still not checked.

choices.text: Paste with Paste Special › Values, then run Circle Invalid Data
choices.why: Right. Values keeps the rules on the cells, and the circles show which pasted values break them.

choices.text: Paste with Ctrl+V twice
choices.why: A plain paste removes the rules from the cells it lands on, however often it is done.
